subsystems.name: Earth-to-orbit transport
subsystems.role: the heavy lift that starts every route; reusable stages bring the cost down enough for regular schedules.

subsystems.name: In-space transfer vehicles
subsystems.role: tugs that move payloads between orbits instead of throwing away a stage on each trip.

subsystems.name: Propellant depots
subsystems.role: store and resell fuel so vehicles can be refuelled in orbit rather than launched fully laden.

subsystems.name: Docking and fluid interfaces
subsystems.role: let any vehicle mate with any depot, tug or habitat, like a standard shipping container.

subsystems.name: Navigation and communications relay
subsystems.role: a schedule is impossible without knowing where everything is and being able to talk to it.

subsystems.name: Surface and salvage elements
subsystems.role: landers, habitats and the equipment that strips derelict hardware for parts and propellant.

subsystems.name: Ground operations and traffic coordination
subsystems.role: flight planning, range safety and shared schedules across many operators.

buildSteps.title: Agree the interfaces first
buildSteps.detail: Publish and adopt one docking and fluid-transfer standard, so hardware from different builders can connect on orbit. Work like this already exists in the International Docking System Standard used on the ISS.

buildSteps.title: Prove refuelling in microgravity
buildSteps.detail: Transfer cryogenic propellant between two tanks in orbit, measuring how much actually arrives. In-space cryogenic transfer is the single hardest missing piece.

buildSteps.title: Build a reusable tug
buildSteps.detail: Design a transfer vehicle that can be refuelled and flown again dozens of times, rather than a one-shot upper stage.

buildSteps.title: Park a depot in a useful orbit
buildSteps.detail: Station propellant, power and spares at a node such as a near-rectilinear halo orbit around the Moon, where many routes can meet.

buildSteps.title: Set up the relay network
buildSteps.detail: Place satellites around the Moon to give continuous communications and navigation, so vehicles are not out of contact behind the far side.

buildSteps.title: Establish a cadence
buildSteps.detail: Fly cargo on a published schedule with reusable launchers, turning launches from events into timetabled freight.

buildSteps.title: Add salvage
buildSteps.detail: Capture spent upper stages and failed spacecraft, drain residual propellant and recycle metal rather than leaving it as debris.

buildSteps.title: Expand the network outward
buildSteps.detail: Replicate depots and relays at Sun–Earth Lagrange points and beyond, using each node as a stepping stone.

prerequisites.why: small-scale and ground-based demonstrations exist, but no routine orbital transfer of liquid hydrogen or oxygen has been proven.
reusable first stages already fly repeatedly; the network needs much higher flight rates and cheaper upper stages.
mechanical docking standards exist, but standardised refuelling and power connections for commercial use do not.
demonstration spacecraft have flown lunar orbits and relay concepts are planned, but no operational constellation covers cislunar space yet.
robotic docking and servicing have been demonstrated in low Earth orbit, not yet reliably at lunar distances.

pathway.milestone: bespoke missions, an internationally agreed docking standard and robotic lunar landers flown by several space agencies and companies
pathway.unlocks: a common mechanical interface and the first lunar surface deliveries.

pathway.milestone: orbital demonstration of propellant transfer, plus lunar relay satellites and a small lunar orbital station
pathway.unlocks: vehicles that can be refuelled, and continuous communications near the Moon.

pathway.milestone: a working depot with a refuellable tug on a published cargo schedule
pathway.unlocks: reuse across routes and a real market for propellant in orbit.

pathway.milestone: routine cislunar cadence with salvage and standardised interfaces
pathway.unlocks: a permanent off-world industrial base and a template for routes to Mars.
